title: Platform traffic decision notebook: tiering, cost-sensitivity, and operator heuristics
author: Morgan Liu
content:
Overview

This notebook captures a compact, operator-friendly decision model for routing, tiering and emergency actioning of LLM inference traffic. It combines an explicit traffic-tier matrix, a numeric Cost-Sensitivity Index (CSI) for tenants/routes, and clear operator heuristics for common platform incidents (token surges, model variant misfires, regional capacity loss). The goal is to provide a single-page reference that on-call operators and product engineers can use to: 1) decide routing adjustments, 2) enact graceful degradation, and 3) quantify expected cost/latency tradeoffs for choices.

Why this exists

- Platform traffic is multi-dimensional: latency SLOs, cost budget, tenant priority, model quality. Operators need a crisp decision surface that maps observability signals to safe actions.
- Many incidents are about tradeoffs (lower cost vs higher latency or slightly reduced quality). This doc standardizes vocabulary and numeric scoring so different operators make consistent choices.

Scope

- Applies to hosted and dedicated runtime pools (all regions).
- Assumes route-level metadata: tenant_id, route_tier, max_token_budget, model_variant, sla_tier.
- Does NOT replace tenant billing policy or contractual SLAs; use this notebook for operational actions when immediate mitigation is needed.

Definitions

- Route: API route /customer/{tenant}/generate or embedding route.
- Route tier: a discrete label {platinum, gold, standard, free}.
- CSI (Cost-Sensitivity Index): 0.0–1.0 numeric score indicating how sensitive a tenant/route is to cost increases (1.0 = very cost-sensitive).
- Latency criticality: {high, medium, low} per route definition.
- Model variant fallback: pre-approved model replacement candidates for quality/cost/latency tradeoffs.

Decision primitives

1) Compute route impact score (RIS): numeric composite used to prioritize actions.

RIS = (SLA_weight * SLA_factor) + (CSI_weight * CSI_factor) + (Burst_weight * Burst_factor) + (Quality_regress_weight * Quality_factor)

- SLA_factor = 1.0 for platinum, 0.7 for gold, 0.4 for standard, 0.1 for free.
- CSI_factor = CSI (0.0–1.0).
- Burst_factor = normalized token surge (0–1) over baseline for route in last 5m.
- Quality_factor = 1 if recent quality alerts triggered for route, else 0.
- Weights (default): SLA_weight=0.4, CSI_weight=0.25, Burst_weight=0.25, Quality_regress_weight=0.1.

Interpretation: RIS in [0,1.0+]; higher RIS -> higher operational priority (prefer fast recovery over cost-saving action).

Traffic tier matrix (operator reference)

| Action category | Preconditions (observability) | Typical operator action | Expected immediate impact | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Emergency failover | Regional capacity loss OR sustained latency p95 > 2*SLO for 5m | Route-level failover to alternate region or standby model pool; enable short-lived bilateral burst credits | Latency drop to within SLO for routes with standby capacity; cost may increase by 10–40% temporarily | Platform Ops |
| Cost-damp mitigation | Token cost spikes across multi-tenant pool, cost burn > 120% of forecasted for hour | Apply per-tenant soft rate-limit; reduce batching window; switch high-CSI tenants to cheaper quantized variant for non-critical routes | Immediate cost reduction; latency +5–15ms | Platform Operators |
| Quality-first rollback | Quality regression alerts triggered for model variant with correlated increased hallucinations | Roll back to previous verified variant; mark suspected model variant restricted for canary traffic | Quality restored; token cost unchanged | Model Onboarding + Platform |
| Graceful degradation | Sustained high queue lengths and rising p99 > 1.5*SLO | Temporarily reduce max allowed sequence length per route; enable prefix-KV cache hints; demote free/standard tier traffic to background queue | Lower p99 tail; higher rejected long-sequence requests for low-tier | Platform Ops |

Operational playbook (step-by-step)

1. Detect: Confirm incident by cross-checking metrics (p50/p95/p99 latency, queue length, token burn rate, model error rate) and alert context. Use the Incident Triage Dashboard (see Dashboards).
2. Score: Compute RIS for top 10 impacted routes. Sort descending.
3. Choose action category using matrix above and context: if regional capacity loss -> Emergency failover; if platform token burn -> Cost-damp mitigation; if model-specific quality alerts -> Quality-first rollback; if tail latency -> Graceful degradation.
4. Execute: Follow runbook snippet below for the chosen action. Document the change in incident ticket with tags: action:, rationale:, expected_impact:, rollback_plan:.
5. Monitor: Watch SLO dashboards and cost delta for 10m, then 30m. If change not improving RIS top 3 routes, escalate to SRE lead.
6. Remediate permanently: If temporary action stayed > 2 hours, schedule follow-up with owning teams and add a task to the platform backlog.

Runbook snippets (CLI and safe checks)

- Emergency region failover (safe mode):

1) Mark affected region read-only in control-plane: `redwoodctl region set-mode --region eu-west-2 --mode read-only --ticket $INC_ID`
2) Move traffic: `redwoodctl route reroute --from-region eu-west-2 --to-region eu-central-1 --match 'tenant in ($IMPACTED)' --max-in-flight 50`
3) Toggle auto-burst to standby: `redwoodctl pool set-burst --pool standby-eu --enabled true --burst-multiplier 2`
4) Validate: check p95 and queue_length for top 5 routes. If p95 still > SLO*1.5, step back and notify SRE lead.

- Cost-damp soft rate-limit (per-route):

1) Identify top 5 cost contributors: query `billing.query.top_token_burn(3600)`
2) For each route where CSI > 0.7 and tier != platinum, apply soft throttling: `redwoodctl route set-rate-limit --route-id $ROUTE --qps 0.8 * current_qps --grace 10s`
3) Notify tenant owner via tenant-notify pipeline: `notify tenant $TENANT --subject "Temporary rate-limits due to platform capacity" --runbook $INC_ID`

SLO / alert mapping (concise)

| Metric | SLO | Alert threshold | Suggested default action |
|---|---:|---|---|
| p95 latency (model gen) | 150ms global hosted gold | p95 > 300ms for 5m | Graceful degradation or failover |
| Queue length (per-pool) | 500 | > 1000 for 3m | Burst credits, prefetch hints, reduce concurrency |
| Token burn rate (global) | forecasted +10% | > forecast*1.2 for 10m | Cost-damp mitigation |
| Model quality regression (eval) | 95% pass on critical eval set | regression > 5% vs baseline | Quality-first rollback |

Dashboards (what to open first)

- Incident Triage Dashboard (operators): single view with top routes by RIS, p95/p99, queue depth, token burn delta.
- Regional Capacity Heatmap: node-level free/used GPU, preemptible share, thermal headroom.
- Token burn leaderboards: rolling 1h/6h/24h with tenant CSI and quotas.
- Model variant canary traces: error rate, divergence, hallucination scoring.

Incident retrospective template (fill after remediation)

1) Summary (1–2 lines)
2) Timeline (epoched events, actions, durations)
3) Root cause (short)
4) What worked well (bulleted)
5) Gaps / surprises (bulleted)
6) Follow-ups (owner, priority, due date)
7) Cost impact estimate (USD, approx)

Example retrospective action items (from a recent dry run)

- Automate RIS computation in triage dashboard (owner: telemetry, P2, due 2026-03-15)
- Add per-tenant soft rate-limit playbook to customer success templates (owner: customer-success, P3)
- Expand standby model pool in eu-central-1 by 20% before Q2 (owner: infra, P1)

Platform roadmap tie-ins (next 12 months)

- Q2 2026: RIS engine GA (server-side scoring + webhook to incident system).
- Q3 2026: Per-route automated soft-mitigations (rate-limit and variant-swap) with audit trails.
- Q4 2026: Cost-aware routing policy (runtime will pick cheaper compatible variant when CSI > 0.8 and latency slack >= 30ms).

Ownership and escalation matrix

- First responder: Platform operator on regional on-call.
- Escalation: SRE lead (after 30m of unsuccessful mitigation) -> Head of Serving Runtime (after 2h) -> Incident commander for customer-impacting outages.

Quick FAQs

Q: When do we prefer model variant fallback vs reducing sequence length?
A: Fallback to a cheaper/quantized variant if quality is acceptable for route (CSI >= 0.6) and latency slack < 30ms. Reduce sequence length if requests are long-tail and route cannot tolerate reduced quality.

Q: How long can temporary measures remain active?
A: Temporary mitigations should be logged and reviewed; if active > 2 hours, file a follow-up action and create a rollback criterion.

Appendix: Example CSI assignment guideline

- Platinum enterprise customer with explicit cost-escalation clause: CSI = 0.2
- Startup on free plan with strict credit limit: CSI = 0.95
- Internal testing tenants: CSI = 0.8

Table: quick numeric reference

| Route tier | SLA_factor | Default CSI | Priority rank baseline |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| platinum | 1.0 | 0.2 | 1 |
| gold | 0.7 | 0.4 | 2 |
| standard | 0.4 | 0.7 | 3 |
| free | 0.1 | 0.95 | 4 |

Contact and feedback

If this notebook is unclear or you observe repeated manual work that could be automated, add an issue to the Platform backlog and tag `triage:operator-notebook`. For urgent changes propose edits directly on this page and ping @Asha.
